deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no derivations or formulas. It is a philosophical-foundational note that continues the previous page, followed by a short dated remark.

(1) Continuation of the previous page. The previous page ends: 'Die Erfindung der Irrational-Zahl ist ... gleichberechtigt u. von gleichem Werthe wie die Erfindung der Differential[-Gleichung-]'. This page begins with 'Rechnung', so the full word is 'Differentialrechnung'. The passage reads: the invention of the irrational number is of equal standing and value with the invention of the differential calculus. As with the calculus, its core is that the inferences which keep recurring are taken in advance and treated once, at the start, in a general form.

Hilbert then puts statements about irrational numbers (defined on the previous page as 'Träger eines Gesetzes', the carrier of a law) on the same footing as all other general theorems. His examples are:
(a) Minkowski's theorem on the 'maximal-minimal content (volume) of convex bodies'. This is presumably Minkowski's convex-body / lattice-point results of 1889-1891, e.g. that a centrally symmetric convex body K in R^n with vol(K) > 2^n contains a nonzero lattice point; the exact intended statement is not specified. Hilbert says such a theorem asserts nothing but: 'if later in my investigation I meet a body which is convex, then its volume ... etc.'
(b) The theorem giving conditions for convergence of a power series, read the same way.

His conclusion is a schematic equation: 'the totality = system of all = each = whenever one is encountered by me'. In modern terms, a universal statement over a totality ('for all x in S, P(x)') is read as a hypothetical, open-ended rule: 'given any x in S, P(x)'. It is not read as a claim about a completed actual infinity. This is the same 'law/rule' reading he applies to irrationals, and it anticipates the hypothetical interpretation of general statements in his 1920s finitism.

(2) 'Antwort auf Studys Brief vom 27/6.91' (answer to Study's letter of 27 June 1891). Hilbert writes: 'Precisely through this shallow manner of fantasizing, as introduced by the school of Klebsch [i.e. Clebsch], the deeper mathematical inventive power is paralysed.' This is a polemical methodological remark, from the context of the invariant-theory disputes of the period. Hilbert's own approach (finiteness theorem, 1888-1890) stood against the computational/symbolic Clebsch-Gordan tradition, which Study partly represented.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there are no computations on the page.
'Klebsch' is Hilbert's own misspelling of Clebsch; he first wrote 'Kleb' and struck it.
The description 'Maximal-Minimal-Inhalt convexer Körper' is vague. It is unclear exactly which theorem of Minkowski is meant (lattice-point theorem, or extremal volume bounds).

deep.surprise_reason: No mathematics proper. It is mildly notable that already in 1891 Hilbert reads universal statements as hypothetical 'whenever I meet one' rules, prefiguring his later finitist stance. However, his early foundational notebook remarks and the anti-Clebsch-school stance are partly known to historians (Rowe, Sieg, Hallett).

checkable.asserts: Illustrative boundary case of Minkowski's theorem: the square [-1,1]^2 has area exactly 2^2 = 4 and contains no nonzero lattice point in its interior, so the bound vol > 2^n is sharp.
Illustrative ratio-test condition for convergence of a power series (sum x^n/n has radius of convergence 1), the kind of general convergence theorem Hilbert cites.
